newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Road-owning company mooted in NZ transport review.
newsitem.headline: Road-owning company mooted in NZ transport review.

text.p: Ownership of New Zealand's roads would be transferred to a state-owned enterprise (SOE) under a proposal in a roads policy review released on Tuesday.
The option is one of five contained in the report which follows a four-year review of land transport pricing.
Releasing the report Transport Minister Jenny Shipley said as the economy grew parts of the road network, valued at NZ$25.8 billion in 1993, were struggling to cope with increased traffic.
"We need to come up with a management and funding system that will meet the demands of the future in an economically sound and sustainable way," she said in a statement.

Shipley said there was evidence that under the current structure -- which draws funds from fuel taxes, heavy vehicle road user charges and local body rates -- some road users were not paying their share.
The report said some district councils spent up to 75 percent of rates income on roads, yet wear and tear was caused by frequent users, not necessarily local ratepayers.

In the 1996/97 year total funding for the road network was $1.3 billion with 23 percent coming from rates, 38 percent from user charges, 26 percent freom petrol tax and 14 percent from vehicle licence fees.
The report said commercial shipping, railways and airline companies had proved a success and it was time to look at whether roads could also be run commercially.
It was also important that road and rail transport companies, in competing for freight, had a level playing field, the report said.
Public submissions are open until August 15. The Government then intends talk to industry group representatives and make final decisions in October.
In response to the report, the Manufacturers Federation said it supported putting all road assets into commercial enterprises jointly owned by central and local government.
"Roading is a watershed issue on whether New Zealanders want to keep our economy more competitive," federation chief executive Simon Arnold said.
He said better investment in roads would deliver substantial benefits.
Jeanette Fitzsimons, co-leader of the Green Party which forms part of the leftwing Alliance grouping, said the report failed to addresss environmental pricing in any of its options.
"This roadbuilding spree will have our cities choking on transport waste," she said in a statement.
